content: 1. Lisinopril should be discontinued as soon as pregnancy is detected to avoid potential harm to the fetus. 2. For patients not receiving a diuretic, the initial dose of lisinopril is 10 mg orally once daily. 3. The usual dosage range for lisinopril is 20-40 mg per day. For patients receiving a diuretic, the initial dose is 5 mg orally once daily. 4. If possible, diuretics should be discontinued for 2-3 days before starting therapy with lisinopril to reduce the risk of hypotension. 5. The maintenance dose of lisinopril is 20-40 mg orally once daily or in two divided doses, with adjustments based on the patient’s response. The maximum dose is 80 mg per day. 6. 7. 8. 9. If a diuretic is used concurrently, its dose should be reduced, if possible, to minimize hypovolemia, which may contribute to hypotension. 10. The occurrence of hypotension after the initial dose of lisinopril does not preclude careful dose titration following effective management of the hypotension. 11. In patients with heart failure and renal impairment or hyponatremia (serum sodium <130 mEq/L), or moderate-to-severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance ≤30 mL/min or serum creatinine >3 mg/dL), therapy with lisinopril should be initiated at a dose of 2.5 mg once daily under close medical supervision. 12. For hemodynamically stable patients within 24 hours of acute myocardial infarction symptoms, the initial dose of lisinopril is 5 mg orally, followed by 5 mg after 24 hours and 10 mg after 48 hours. The maintenance dose is 10 mg orally once daily for six weeks. 13. Patients should also receive standard recommended treatments, such as thrombolytics, aspirin, and beta-blockers, as appropriate. 14.5 mg oral dose of lisinopril. 15.5 mg if needed. 16. 17. In patients with acute myocardial infarction and evidence of renal dysfunction (serum creatinine >2 mg/dL), lisinopril should be initiated cautiously. 18. If renal dysfunction develops during lisinopril treatment (serum creatinine >3 mg/dL or doubling from baseline), withdrawal of the drug should be considered. 19. Patients with hereditary or idiopathic angioedema should not receive lisinopril due to the risk of severe adverse reactions. 20. Angioedema involving the face, extremities, lips, tongue, glottis, or larynx has been reported in patients treated with ACE inhibitors, including lisinopril. This can occur at any time during treatment. 21. Black patients have a higher risk of angioedema with ACE inhibitors compared to non-Black patients. 22. If angioedema occurs, lisinopril should be promptly discontinued, and appropriate therapy and monitoring should be provided until complete resolution of symptoms. 23. Even in cases where only tongue swelling occurs without respiratory distress, prolonged observation may be required as antihistamines and corticosteroids may not be sufficient. 24. Rarely, fatalities have been reported due to angioedema associated with laryngeal or tongue edema. 25. Patients with tongue, glottis, or larynx involvement are at risk of airway obstruction, particularly those with a history of airway surgery. 26. In cases of airway obstruction, appropriate therapy, such as subcutaneous epinephrine (1:1000 solution, 0.3-0. 27. Intestinal angioedema has been reported in patients treated with ACE inhibitors, presenting with abdominal pain, with or without nausea or vomiting, and resolving after discontinuation of the ACE inhibitor. 28. Anaphylactoid reactions have been reported during desensitization treatments with hymenoptera venom in patients receiving ACE inhibitors. These reactions were avoided when ACE inhibitors were temporarily withheld. 29. Sudden and potentially life-threatening anaphylactoid reactions have been reported in patients undergoing dialysis with high-flux membranes while on ACE inhibitors. Dialysis must be stopped immediately, and aggressive therapy for anaphylactoid reactions should be initiated. 30. Excessive hypotension is rare in patients with uncomplicated hypertension treated with lisinopril alone. 31. 32. 33. In such patients, it may be advisable to reduce or discontinue diuretics or cautiously increase salt intake before initiating lisinopril therapy. 34. 35. Therapy with lisinopril should be initiated under close medical supervision in patients at risk of excessive hypotension, and these patients should be closely monitored during the first two weeks of treatment and whenever the dose is increased. 36. Hyperkalemia (serum potassium >5.7 mEq/L) occurred in approximately 2.2% of hypertensive patients and 4.8% of heart failure patients in clinical trials. 37. Risk factors for hyperkalemia include renal insufficiency, diabetes mellitus, and the concomitant use of potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, or potassium-containing salt substitutes. 38. Hyperkalemia can cause serious, sometimes fatal, arrhythmias. Lisinopril should be used cautiously, if at all, with these agents, and frequent monitoring of serum potassium is recommended. 39. Persistent nonproductive cough has been reported with all ACE inhibitors, including lisinopril, and resolves after discontinuation of therapy. 40. ACE inhibitor-induced cough should be considered in the differential diagnosis of cough. 41. Rarely, ACE inhibitors have been associated with a syndrome starting with cholestatic jaundice or hepatitis and progressing to fulminant hepatic necrosis and sometimes death. 42. Patients receiving ACE inhibitors who develop jaundice or marked elevations of hepatic enzymes should discontinue the drug and receive appropriate medical follow-up. 43. In patients with severe congestive heart failure whose renal function may depend on the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, treatment with ACE inhibitors may be associated with oliguria, progressive azotemia, and, rarely, acute renal failure or death. 44. In hypertensive patients with renal artery stenosis, increases in blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine may occur, which are usually reversible upon discontinuation of lisinopril and/or diuretic therapy. 45. Patients with pre-existing renal impairment are more likely to develop increases in blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine. Dosage reduction or discontinuation of lisinopril and/or diuretics may be required. 46. In clinical trials, hyperkalemia was a cause for discontinuation of therapy in approximately 0.1% of hypertensive patients, 0.6% of heart failure patients, and 0.1% of myocardial infarction patients. 47. Increases in blood urea nitrogen or serum creatinine were a cause for discontinuation in 1.2% of patients. 48. Small decreases in hemoglobin and hematocrit frequently occur in patients treated with lisinopril but are rarely of clinical importance unless another cause of anemia coexists. 49. Rare cases of bone marrow depression, hemolytic anemia, leukopenia/neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia have been reported. 50. Elevations of liver enzymes and/or serum bilirubin have occurred and should prompt discontinuation of lisinopril if significant.
